why: Every security budget, audit plan and supplier contract starts from one question: which risks matter most, and what do we do about them? GRC analysts run the risk assessments, keep the risk register alive and turn technical findings into decisions that managers can sign. It is the core skill behind ISO/IEC 27001, NIS2 and DORA work, and interviews test it with real cases.
outcome: describe a risk with the right vocabulary, choose and explain a method (ISO/IEC 27005, EBIOS Risk Manager, NIST SP 800-30, FAIR), score and map risks without false precision, keep a useful risk register, propose treatments and compute residual risk, report against the risk appetite, assess suppliers, and run a business impact analysis with RTO and RPO.

lessons.title: Risk vocabulary: asset, threat, vulnerability, impact
text: A risk is the possibility that an event harms what the organisation values. In information security, ISO/IEC 27000 defines risk as the effect of uncertainty on objectives, and in practice a risk is described by a scenario: a threat exploits a vulnerability of an asset, which causes an impact. The likelihood says how plausible the scenario is; the impact says how bad it would be.

An asset is anything of value: information (customer data, payroll files, source code), the processes that use it (payments, payroll) and the supporting assets they run on (servers, applications, people, buildings, suppliers). A threat is what could cause harm: an attacker, a careless employee, a flood, a supplier failure. A vulnerability is a weakness a threat can use: a missing patch, a shared admin password, no MFA, a server room in a basement. A threat without a vulnerability, or a vulnerability no threat can reach, is not much of a risk.

Write each risk as one sentence that a manager can understand: “Because of <cause or vulnerability>, <threat> could <event>, leading to <impact on the business>.” Avoid vague titles like “cyber risk” or “GDPR”: they cannot be scored, owned or treated. A good risk statement names the asset and the business consequence in money, days of downtime, number of people affected or legal exposure.

Inherent risk is the level of risk before controls are taken into account (some teams say “gross risk”). Residual risk is what remains after the controls in place, or after the planned treatment. Organisations define these terms slightly differently (some add a “current risk” between the two), so check the methodology of the company and use its words. The gap between inherent and residual risk shows how much the controls are worth, and which controls must not fail.

Interviewers often ask you to tell a threat from a vulnerability, or to turn a technical finding into a risk. A penetration test finding such as “the VPN appliance is two years behind on patches” is a vulnerability; the risk is the scenario it enables, for example ransomware entering through the VPN and stopping production for a week.
points: Risk = scenario: a threat exploits a vulnerability of an asset and causes an impact.
Likelihood = how plausible; impact = how bad (money, downtime, people, legal).
Write risk statements: because of… could… leading to…
Inherent risk = before controls; residual risk = after controls or treatment.
A finding (missing patch) is a vulnerability, not yet a risk.

example.code:
Asset          Customer database (CRM, 80,000 customer records)
Threat         External attacker using stolen passwords
Vulnerability  No MFA on CRM administrator accounts
Event          Bulk export of customer data
Impact         Personal data breach, notification, fines, lost customers

Risk statement
  Because CRM admin accounts have no MFA, an attacker with stolen
  passwords could export customer data, leading to a notifiable
  personal data breach and a loss of customer trust.

Inherent risk  Likelihood 4 x Impact 5 = 20
Residual risk  Likelihood 2 x Impact 5 = 10   (after MFA + export alerts)
example.note: The MFA control lowers the likelihood, not the impact: if the export happens anyway, the damage is the same. That is why the impact stays at 5.

lessons.title: Risk methods: ISO/IEC 27005, EBIOS RM, NIST SP 800-30 and FAIR
text: ISO/IEC 27005 gives guidance for information security risk management and supports the risk assessment and treatment that ISO/IEC 27001 requires (clauses 6.1.2 and 6.1.3, then 8.2 and 8.3). It follows the ISO 31000 process: establish the context and the risk criteria, identify, analyse and evaluate the risks, treat them, then monitor, review and communicate. The 2022 edition describes two ways to identify risks: event-based (start from risk sources and events) and asset-based (start from assets, threats and vulnerabilities).

EBIOS Risk Manager is the French method published by ANSSI, widely used in the French public sector, by operators of essential services and by large companies. It runs in five workshops: scope and security baseline, risk origins (who could attack and why), strategic scenarios (the paths through the ecosystem, including suppliers and partners), operational scenarios (the technical attack steps) and risk treatment. Its strength is to think like an attacker and to include the ecosystem; it uses gravity (gravité) and likelihood (vraisemblance) scales.

NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1, “Guide for Conducting Risk Assessments”, is the US reference. Its process has four steps: prepare the assessment, conduct it (threat sources and events, vulnerabilities, likelihood, impact, risk), communicate the results and maintain the assessment. It fits the NIST Risk Management Framework and is common in US-linked companies.

These methods are mostly qualitative: they rate likelihood and impact on scales (low to very high, or 1 to 5). Quantitative analysis expresses risk in money. The classic formulas are single loss expectancy SLE = asset value × exposure factor, and annualised loss expectancy ALE = SLE × ARO (annual rate of occurrence). FAIR (Factor Analysis of Information Risk, an Open Group standard known as Open FAIR) goes further: it estimates loss event frequency and loss magnitude as ranges, then runs simulations to give a distribution of annual loss. It needs data and time, so teams usually keep it for the few risks where a money figure helps a decision, such as buying cyber insurance or funding a large project.

In practice, most companies use a simplified in-house method inspired by one of these. What interviewers want is that you can name them correctly, explain the differences in one sentence each, and say which one you would use: ISO/IEC 27005 for an ISO 27001 scope, EBIOS RM when a French regulator or client expects it, FAIR when management asks “how much could we lose?”.
points: ISO/IEC 27005: guidance for the ISO 27001 risk process, following ISO 31000.
EBIOS Risk Manager (ANSSI): five workshops, attacker and ecosystem view.
NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1: prepare, conduct, communicate, maintain.
ALE = SLE × ARO; SLE = asset value × exposure factor.
FAIR: quantitative, frequency and magnitude as ranges, for the decisions that need money.

example.code:
ISO/IEC 27005        ISO guidance for information security risk
                     (the risk process behind ISO/IEC 27001 clauses 6.1.2 and 8.2)
EBIOS Risk Manager   ANSSI method (France), 5 workshops:
                       1 Scope and security baseline
                       2 Risk origins
                       3 Strategic scenarios
                       4 Operational scenarios
                       5 Risk treatment
NIST SP 800-30 Rev.1 Prepare -> Conduct -> Communicate -> Maintain
FAIR (Open FAIR)     Risk = loss event frequency x loss magnitude,
                     as ranges in EUR per year (quantitative)
example.note: Know one line on each method; in an interview, say which one fits the context rather than which one is best.

lessons.title: Scoring risks and the heat map
text: A scoring scale turns opinions into comparable numbers. The common choice is 1 to 5 for likelihood and 1 to 5 for impact, so the risk score = likelihood × impact goes from 1 to 25. Each level must be defined in words the business shares: likelihood 4 = “likely: expected once in the next 1 to 3 years”; impact 5 = “severe: loss above 5 M EUR, more than a week of downtime of a critical process, or regulatory sanctions”. Without definitions, two people score the same risk 2 and 4.

Impact usually has several columns: financial, operational (downtime), legal and regulatory, reputation, people (health and safety). The rule is to take the highest one: a data breach with little direct cost but a notification to the data protection authority and press coverage is still a 4 or 5.

The heat map draws the risks on a grid, likelihood on one axis and impact on the other, coloured by bands such as low (1 to 4), medium (5 to 9), high (10 to 16) and critical (20 to 25). Each band has a rule: who must know, how fast to treat, who can accept. Showing two maps, inherent and residual, makes the value of the controls visible in one look.

Beware of false precision. Scores on ordinal scales are rankings, not measures: a 20 is not exactly twice as bad as a 10, and 5 × 4 and 4 × 5 give the same score for very different risks (frequent and serious, or rare and catastrophic). Do not average scores, do not add them up into a “total risk”, and do not show decimals. Discuss the borderline cases instead of hiding them behind a number, and for big decisions switch to ranges in money.

Scoring is a group exercise. Run it with the risk owner, the IT or security expert and someone who knows the business process; record the reasons for each score in the register (“likelihood 4: two similar incidents in the sector last year, VPN still unpatched”). The next reviewer, or the auditor, will ask why.
points: Define each level of each scale in business words.
Impact: take the highest of financial, operational, legal, reputation, people.
Score = likelihood × impact, 1 to 25; bands decide who acts and how fast.
Ordinal scores rank risks: no averages, no totals, no decimals.
Write down the reason for each score.

example.note: D2 the score, E2 the band, H2 the number of critical risks, H3 the open risks above the appetite in G1. The $ keeps G1 fixed when the formula is copied.

lessons.title: The risk register
text: The risk register is the single list of the organisation’s risks, their scores, owners and treatments. It can be a spreadsheet, a GRC tool (ServiceNow IRM, Archer, OneTrust and others) or a page in the ISMS; auditors care less about the tool than about whether it is complete, current and used for decisions.

Typical fields: ID, title, risk statement, category (cyber, third party, compliance, availability…), asset or process, risk owner, inherent likelihood, impact and score, existing controls, residual likelihood, impact and score, treatment decision, action plan with action owner and due date, target score, status, date of the last review and date of the next one. Link each risk to its controls and, for ISO 27001, to the Statement of Applicability.

The risk owner is the person accountable for the risk and with the authority to decide on it, usually a business or department head, not the CISO and not the GRC analyst. ISO/IEC 27001 asks that risk owners be identified and that they approve the treatment plan and accept the residual risks. The analyst facilitates, challenges and keeps the register; the owner decides and is accountable.

Review cadence depends on the level: critical and high risks every month or quarter, others at least once a year, and at once when something changes (an incident, a new system, a new supplier, a new law, an audit finding). A register that is updated only before the audit is dead: the auditor sees it from the review dates and from actions overdue for months.

Common problems: risks written as controls (“no SIEM”), duplicates of the same scenario under different names, owners who left the company, actions with no date, and closed risks deleted instead of archived. Keep the history: a risk that goes from 16 to 8 after a project is the best proof that the programme works.
points: One register: statement, owner, inherent and residual scores, controls, decision, actions, dates.
The risk owner is a business manager who decides; the analyst facilitates.
Review high risks monthly or quarterly, others yearly, and after any change.
Archive closed risks; keep the score history.

example.code:
ID              R-07
Title           Payroll SaaS outage at month end
Risk statement  Because payroll runs on one SaaS provider with no tested
                fallback, an outage in the last 3 days of the month could
                delay salaries for 1,200 staff (legal and social impact).
Category        Third party / availability
Process         Monthly payroll
Risk owner      HR director
Inherent        L 3 x I 4 = 12   High
Controls        Provider SLA 99.5 %, payroll file exported on D-5
Residual        L 2 x I 4 = 8    Medium
Decision        Modify: manual fallback procedure, tested before 30 June
Action owner    Payroll manager      Due 2026-06-30   Status: In progress
Last review     2026-03-15           Next review: 2026-06-15 (quarterly)
example.note: The owner is the HR director, who bears the business impact; the payroll manager carries out the action.

lessons.title: Treating risks and accepting residual risk
text: ISO/IEC 27005 names four treatment options: risk modification (change the likelihood or the impact with controls), risk retention (accept it knowingly), risk avoidance (stop the activity or change it so the risk disappears) and risk sharing (share it with another party, through insurance or a contract). ISO 31000 describes the same choices in more detail. Many US and older texts say mitigate, accept, avoid and transfer; use the company’s words, and know both.

Sharing does not remove accountability. Cyber insurance pays part of the cost of an incident but does not prevent it, does not cover every loss (fines are often excluded or not insurable) and does not protect the reputation. Outsourcing a service to a provider moves the operations, not the responsibility: under GDPR, the controller remains responsible for the personal data its processors handle.

To modify a risk, choose controls that act on the scenario: preventive ones lower the likelihood (MFA, patching, network segmentation), detective ones shorten the attack (alerts, log monitoring), corrective ones reduce the impact (offline backups, a recovery plan). ISO/IEC 27001 Annex A lists 93 controls in its 2022 edition, useful as a checklist; compare the cost of each control with the risk it removes.

Residual risk is the new score once the controls work. Some teams re-score likelihood and impact directly; others use a simple convention such as residual = inherent × (1 − control effectiveness), so a risk of 20 with controls rated 60 % effective ends at 8. Either way, base the effectiveness on evidence (tests, audits, incident data), not on the control’s existence: a backup never restored is not 90 % effective.

Risk acceptance is a formal decision. The person who accepts must have authority for that level (often the risk owner below the appetite, the executive committee above it), understand the scenario and the cost of the options, and sign with a date, conditions and an expiry date, for example six months or until a migration. Record it in the register and review it before it expires. ISO/IEC 27001 requires the risk owners to accept the residual risks.
points: Four options: modify (reduce), retain (accept), avoid, share (transfer).
Insurance and outsourcing share the cost, not the accountability.
Pick controls on the scenario: preventive, detective, corrective.
Residual = inherent × (1 − effectiveness) is one convention; base effectiveness on evidence.
Acceptance: right authority, signed, with conditions and an expiry date.

example.code:
ISO 31000 / 27005   Common US wording   Example
Modify (reduce)     Mitigate            Enforce MFA, patch, segment the network
Retain (accept)     Accept              Keep the old intranet until Q3 retirement
Avoid               Avoid               Stop storing card numbers: use tokens
Share               Transfer            Cyber insurance, contract with a provider

Residual score = inherent score x (1 - control effectiveness)
               = 20 x (1 - 0.6) = 8
example.note: The ISO words (modify, retain, avoid, share) and the common words (mitigate, accept, avoid, transfer) describe the same four choices.

lessons.title: Risk appetite and reporting to management
text: Risk appetite is the amount and type of risk an organisation is willing to pursue or keep to reach its objectives. It is set by top management or the board, and it turns into rules the analyst can apply: “no residual cyber risk above 12 without executive committee acceptance”, “no critical supplier without an exit plan”, “no personal data outside the EU without approved safeguards”. Risk tolerance (or thresholds) is the acceptable variation around it, often expressed with key risk indicators (KRIs).

Appetite differs by domain. A bank may have a low appetite for regulatory and cyber risk and a higher one for trying new products; a start-up may accept more availability risk on internal tools than on its customer platform. The appetite also decides the authority: below it, the risk owner can accept; above it, the risk goes to the executive committee with options.

KRIs are measurable signals that a risk is growing: the share of critical vulnerabilities not patched within 30 days, the number of admin accounts without MFA, the share of critical suppliers not reassessed this year, backup restore tests failed. Each KRI has a threshold (green, amber, red) linked to the appetite, so the report shows trends before an incident does.

Management wants decisions, not a 300-line register. A good report fits on one or two pages: the top risks with residual score, trend and position against the appetite; what changed since last time; overdue actions; acceptances that expire; and the decisions asked of the reader, with options and costs. Use the heat map once, plain business language everywhere, and the same format every quarter so trends are easy to read.

For the board or the audit committee, link risks to the objectives they threaten and to regulations that name management’s responsibility: NIS2 makes management bodies of essential and important entities approve cybersecurity risk measures and follow training, and DORA gives the management body of financial entities the final responsibility for ICT risk.
points: Appetite: how much risk management accepts, written as rules.
Below the appetite the owner decides; above it, escalate with options.
KRIs with thresholds show a risk growing before the incident.
Report: top risks, trend, appetite, overdue actions, expiring acceptances, decisions asked.
NIS2 and DORA put cyber risk on management’s desk.

example.code:
Top risks - Q2 report to the risk committee
ID    Risk                        Residual  Trend  Appetite (12)  Action
R-12  Ransomware on plants        16        =      above          EDR rollout 70 %, due Sept
R-21  Privileged access misuse    15        up     above          PAM project delayed
R-07  Payroll SaaS outage          8        down   within         Fallback tested 2 June
Overdue actions: 3 of 41     Acceptances expiring this quarter: 2
Decision asked: fund the PAM project, or accept R-21 formally until Q4
example.note: End every report with the decision you need; a report without a request is read and forgotten.

lessons.title: Third-party and supplier risk
text: Suppliers hold data, run services and connect to networks, so their weaknesses become yours: many large incidents started at a provider. Third-party risk management (TPRM) covers the whole life of the relationship: inventory and tiering, due diligence before signing, contract clauses, monitoring during the contract and a clean exit.

Start with an inventory and tier the suppliers by inherent risk: which data they access (personal, financial, health), how critical the service is, what network access they have and how hard they would be to replace. A payroll SaaS with all employee data is tier 1; a print shop with no data is tier 3. The tier decides the depth of the checks, because no team can assess 800 suppliers in depth.

Due diligence combines a questionnaire and evidence. Common questionnaire bases are the Shared Assessments SIG and the Cloud Security Alliance CAIQ; French clients often add a security assurance plan (plan d’assurance sécurité, PAS) to the contract. Evidence carries more weight than answers: a SOC 2 Type II report (an auditor’s opinion on the operating effectiveness of controls over a period, often 6 to 12 months, while Type I covers only the design at one date) or an ISO/IEC 27001 certificate. Check the scope (does it cover the service you buy?), the dates, the exceptions in the SOC 2 report and the complementary user entity controls you must run yourself.

Contract clauses turn expectations into obligations: security requirements, breach notification within a set time, right to audit, list and approval of subcontractors (fourth parties), data location, backup and continuity commitments, SLAs, and an exit or reversibility clause with data return and deletion. For personal data, GDPR Article 28 sets the content of the processing agreement; financial entities under DORA must also keep a register of information on all their ICT third-party arrangements.

Monitoring continues after signature: reassess tier 1 suppliers yearly, follow certificate expiry and new SOC 2 reports, watch for breaches in the news and for security ratings where the company uses them, and review the supplier after any incident. Look at concentration risk too: when many critical services depend on one cloud provider or one software vendor, a single outage stops them all, and an exit plan becomes a real requirement.
points: Tier suppliers by data, criticality, access and substitutability.
Questionnaire (SIG, CAIQ) + evidence: SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001 certificate, with scope checked.
Contract: security, breach notification, audit right, subcontractors, exit; GDPR Art. 28 for processors.
Monitor continuously; reassess tier 1 yearly.
Concentration risk: too many critical services on one provider.

example.code:
Tier 1  critical service, or sensitive data at scale
        questionnaire (SIG or CAIQ based) + evidence: SOC 2 Type II report
        or ISO/IEC 27001 certificate (check the scope), pen test summary,
        BCP test results; security clauses in the contract;
        reassessed every year, monitored continuously
Tier 2  some personal data, or a service that is useful but replaceable
        short questionnaire + certificate, reassessed every 2 years
Tier 3  no data, no access, easy to replace
        basic checks (company, sanctions, standard terms)
example.note: The depth of the checks follows the tier: spend the effort where the data and the dependency are.

lessons.title: Business continuity and resilience
text: Business continuity keeps the critical activities running, at an acceptable level, during and after a disruption: a ransomware attack, a data centre fire, a supplier failure, a pandemic. ISO 22301 sets the requirements of a business continuity management system (BCMS), and resilience regulations (NIS2, DORA for finance) ask for tested continuity and recovery plans.

The business impact analysis (BIA) comes first. For each activity, it asks what happens over time if it stops: after 4 hours, 1 day, 1 week, in money, legal exposure, customers and safety. From this come the maximum tolerable period of disruption (MTPD, when the impact becomes unacceptable), the recovery time objective (RTO, how fast the activity or system must be back, shorter than the MTPD) and the recovery point objective (RPO, how much data, measured in time, can be lost). The BIA also lists the dependencies: systems, people, sites, suppliers. In France, teams often say DMIA and PDMA for the maximum downtime and maximum data loss.

RTO and RPO drive the technical choices. An RPO of 24 hours allows nightly backups; an RPO of near zero needs replication. An RTO of 2 hours needs a standby system ready to switch; an RTO of 3 days can accept a rebuild from backups. Tighter objectives cost more, so the business must justify them with the BIA, not ask for “zero” everywhere.

The business continuity plan (BCP, plan de continuité d’activité in French) says how the business keeps working: workarounds, alternative sites, manual procedures, crisis team and communication. The disaster recovery plan (DRP, plan de reprise d’activité) says how IT restores the systems and data. A crisis management plan sits above both: who decides, who talks to staff, customers, authorities and the press.

An untested plan is a hope. Test it at several levels: a walkthrough of the document, a tabletop exercise on a scenario (for example ransomware on a Friday night), technical tests such as restoring backups and failing over to the standby site, and from time to time a full exercise. Compare the measured recovery time with the RTO, record the gaps as actions, and update the plan after every test, incident and major change.
points: BIA first: impact over time, MTPD, RTO, RPO, dependencies.
RTO = how fast back; RPO = how much data lost, in time.
BCP keeps the business working; DRP restores IT; crisis management decides and communicates.
ISO 22301 sets the requirements of a business continuity management system.
Test (tabletop, restore, failover), compare with the RTO, fix the gaps.

example.code:
Process         MTPD     RTO      RPO      Depends on
Card payments   4 h      2 h      0        payment gateway, order DB, network
Payroll         3 days   1 day    24 h     payroll SaaS, HR file share
Intranet        1 week   3 days   24 h     web server, CMS database

Checks: RTO < MTPD for every process
        backup or replication frequency meets the RPO
        recovery time measured in the last test <= RTO
example.note: Card payments need replication (RPO 0) and a standby gateway (RTO 2 h); payroll can rebuild from a daily backup within a day.

pitfalls: Vague risks such as “cyber attack” or “GDPR” that cannot be scored, owned or treated: write a scenario with a business impact.
Scales without definitions, so every workshop scores the same risk differently.
Averaging or adding ordinal scores, or showing decimals: false precision that hides the real discussion.
Making the CISO or the GRC analyst the owner of every risk: the business owner must decide and accept.
Counting a control as effective because it exists, without tests or evidence.
Accepting a high risk by e-mail, without the right authority, conditions or expiry date.
Trusting a supplier’s ISO 27001 certificate or SOC 2 report without checking its scope, dates and exceptions.

exercises.q: In D2, the inherent score of the ransomware risk (likelihood × impact).
exercises.hint: Score = likelihood × impact. Use the cells.
exercises.explain: 4 × 5 = 20, a critical risk on a 1-to-25 scale. Copied down, the formula gives 6 for laptop theft and 8 for the payroll outage.

exercises.q: In E2, the residual score of the ransomware risk, using residual = inherent × (1 − control effectiveness).
exercises.hint: Multiply the inherent score by the share the control does not remove.
exercises.explain: 20 × (1 − 0.6) = 8. This is one convention among others: the effectiveness rate should come from tests and evidence, not from the control merely existing.

exercises.q: The appetite is in F2. In G2, count the risks that are still Open and whose residual score is above the appetite.
exercises.hint: COUNTIFS with two criteria: ">"&F2 on the scores and "Open" on the status.
exercises.explain: R-02 (16) and R-06 (20) are open and above 12; R-04 (15) is above but closed. Answer: 2. Building the criterion with ">"&F2 keeps the count right when the appetite changes.

exercises.q: In E2, the annualised loss expectancy of the ransomware scenario (ALE = asset value × exposure factor × ARO).
exercises.hint: SLE = asset value × exposure factor; ALE = SLE × ARO.
exercises.explain: SLE = 2,000,000 × 0.25 = 500,000 EUR per occurrence; ALE = 500,000 × 0.2 = 100,000 EUR per year. Compare it with the yearly cost of a control: a control costing 40,000 EUR a year that halves the ARO saves 50,000 EUR a year.

exercises.q: In F2, the name of the supplier with the highest risk score, with INDEX and MATCH.
exercises.hint: MATCH(MAX(D2:D6),D2:D6,0) finds the row of the highest score; INDEX returns the name from column A.
exercises.explain: The highest score is 16, so the answer is HR-Soft. XLOOKUP(MAX(D2:D6),D2:D6,A2:A6) works too. With a tie, MATCH returns the first one: check the list for ties before reporting a single name.

exercises.q: In D2, write "OK" if the tested recovery time meets the RTO, otherwise "Gap".
exercises.explain: The payment gateway took 6 hours to recover against an RTO of 4: Gap. Each gap becomes an action (standby system, automated failover) or a business decision to change the RTO, backed by the BIA.

exercises.q: Match each treatment option with an example.
pairs: Enforce MFA on all remote access
Keep the legacy intranet unpatched until it is retired in 3 months, signed by its owner
Drop the plan to store card numbers and use the payment provider’s tokens
Buy a cyber insurance policy covering incident response costs
exercises.answer: Modify acts on likelihood or impact with controls; retain is a signed decision to keep the risk; avoid removes the activity that creates it; share moves part of the cost to an insurer or a contract, not the accountability.

exercises.q: Sort these items into threats and vulnerabilities.

groups.name: Vulnerability
items: Backups on the same network as the servers

exercises.answer: A threat is what could cause harm; a vulnerability is the weakness it uses. The flood is the threat; the basement server room is the weakness that turns it into a risk.

exercises.q: Put the risk management process in order (ISO 31000 / ISO 27005).
steps: Establish the context and the risk criteria
Evaluate the risks against the criteria
exercises.answer: Context and criteria come first, otherwise scores mean nothing. Identification, analysis and evaluation form the risk assessment; treatment follows; monitoring and communication run all along and start the next cycle.

exercises.q: The sales director owns risk R-31: the customer portal runs on an unsupported framework (residual score 20, appetite 12). Fixing it costs 80,000 EUR and he wants to accept the risk.

choices.label: Check who can accept a risk at this level under the policy, and make sure he understands the scenario and its impact
choices.feedback: Acceptance is valid only from the right authority and with an informed owner.

choices.label: Record the acceptance in the register: it is his risk
choices.feedback: He owns the risk, but a risk above the appetite usually needs a higher authority to accept it.

choices.label: Refuse: a high risk can never be accepted
choices.feedback: Accepting a high risk is possible at the right level. GRC advises and escalates; it does not veto business decisions.

steps.text: The policy says risks above 12 need executive committee acceptance. Next?

choices.label: Prepare a short decision paper: scenario, score, options with costs (for example a WAF and isolation now for 15,000 EUR, migration next year), the owner’s view and an expiry date
choices.feedback: The committee can decide only between clear options with costs.

choices.label: E-mail the CEO that the sales director is taking dangerous risks
choices.feedback: This damages the relationship and gives no options: escalation is a process, not a complaint.

steps.text: The committee accepts the risk for 6 months, on condition that the WAF is deployed. What do you record?

choices.label: The acceptance in the register: who signed, date, conditions, expiry date and review; the WAF as a tracked action
choices.feedback: An accepted risk stays open and is reviewed before the acceptance expires.

choices.label: Close the risk: it has been accepted
choices.feedback: An accepted risk still exists; closing it hides it from the next reviews.

exercises.answer: Check the authority, inform the owner, escalate above the appetite with costed options, and record a signed acceptance with conditions and an expiry date. The risk stays in the register and is reviewed.

exercises.q: The order database is backed up every night at 01:00 and nothing else. It fails at 17:00 and is restored from the last backup. What is the main problem?
options: Up to 16 hours of orders are lost: the RPO is too long for this process
The restore takes 16 hours: the RTO is missed
Nothing: nightly backups meet any RPO
The MTPD is exceeded by definition
exercises.answer: The RPO measures the data lost, in time, since the last good copy: here 16 hours of orders. The RTO is about how long the restore takes, which the question does not give. A shorter RPO needs more frequent backups or replication.

exercises.q: A stolen unencrypted laptop costs 50,000 EUR per incident (SLE) and happens 0.2 times a year (ARO). What is the ALE, in EUR per year?
exercises.answer: ALE = SLE × ARO = 50,000 × 0.2 = 10,000 EUR per year. Disk encryption on 300 laptops costing less than that per year pays for itself on this risk alone.

exercises.q: A small online shop (25 staff, card payments through a payment provider, customer accounts, warehouse software in the cloud) asks you for its first risk register. Write three entries: risk statement, owner, inherent score, controls, residual score and decision.
exercises.answer: 1) Because staff e-mail has no MFA and phishing is frequent, an attacker could take over the admin account of the shop platform and steal customer data, leading to a GDPR breach and lost sales. Owner: managing director. Inherent L4 × I4 = 16. Controls: MFA on e-mail and the shop admin, phishing training. Residual L2 × I4 = 8. Decision: modify, MFA within one month. 2) Because the warehouse software runs at a single cloud supplier with no tested exit or export, an outage of more than two days could stop shipping in the peak season, leading to cancelled orders. Owner: operations manager. Inherent L3 × I4 = 12. Controls: SLA, daily data export, manual picking procedure. Residual L2 × I3 = 6. Decision: modify, then share part of the cost through the contract (service credits). 3) Because the shop server is two versions behind on security patches, ransomware could encrypt the site and its database, leading to several days offline. Owner: CTO or head of IT. Inherent L4 × I5 = 20. Controls: monthly patching, offline backups restored every quarter, EDR. Residual L2 × I4 = 8. Decision: modify; if patching cannot follow, accept for a limited time with the managing director’s signature and an expiry date. Each entry names a business owner, a dated action and a next review.

interview.q: Walk me through how you would run a risk assessment for a new application.
interview.a: I agree the scope and the criteria first: which processes and data the application supports, the scales and the appetite. With the business owner and the technical team I identify the assets, the threats and the vulnerabilities, including the hosting provider and integrations, and write each risk as a scenario with a business impact. We score likelihood and impact with the defined scales and record the reasons, compare with the appetite, and agree treatments with owners and dates. The results go into the register, residual risks are accepted by the right person, and I plan a review before go-live and after major changes.

interview.q: What is the difference between inherent and residual risk, and why do both matter?
interview.a: Inherent risk is the level before controls are taken into account; residual risk is what remains with the controls in place or after treatment. Residual risk is what management accepts. Inherent risk shows how much depends on the controls: a risk that drops from 20 to 6 means those controls are critical and must be tested and monitored, because if they fail the risk goes back to 20.

interview.q: Which risk method would you use, and why?
interview.a: It depends on the context. For an ISO/IEC 27001 scope, a process aligned with ISO/IEC 27005 and ISO 31000. If a French regulator or a public-sector client expects it, EBIOS Risk Manager, which also works well for attack scenarios through suppliers. In a US-oriented company, NIST SP 800-30. When management needs a money figure, for example to size cyber insurance, a quantitative analysis such as FAIR on a few key scenarios. In practice I adapt to the company’s methodology and make sure the scales are defined and applied consistently.

interview.q: A business owner wants to accept a risk well above the appetite. What do you do?
interview.a: I do not refuse, and I do not simply record it. I make sure the owner understands the scenario and its impact, check who has authority for that level under the policy, and prepare the decision for that authority with costed options: full fix, a cheaper interim control, or acceptance. If acceptance is chosen, it is signed with conditions and an expiry date, the risk stays open in the register and I review it before it expires.

interview.q: How do you assess a new SaaS supplier that will process customer data?
interview.a: I tier it first: customer personal data and a critical service make it tier 1. Then due diligence: a questionnaire based on SIG or CAIQ, and evidence such as a SOC 2 Type II report or an ISO/IEC 27001 certificate, checking scope, dates, exceptions and the controls left to us. I review data location and subcontractors, and with legal I make sure the contract has the GDPR Article 28 terms, breach notification, audit rights and exit. Gaps go into the risk register with an owner, and the supplier is reassessed every year and monitored in between.

interview.q: Explain RTO and RPO, and how they are set.
interview.a: The RTO is how quickly a process or system must be back after a disruption; the RPO is how much data, measured in time, we can afford to lose. They come from the business impact analysis: how the impact grows over time and the maximum tolerable period of disruption, so the RTO must be shorter than that. They drive the design: an RPO near zero needs replication, a short RTO a standby system. Then we test, compare the measured recovery time with the RTO and fix the gaps.

interview.q: How do you report risks to management?
interview.a: On one or two pages: the top risks with residual score, trend and position against the appetite, what changed since last time, overdue actions, acceptances about to expire, and the decisions I need from them, with options and costs. I use plain business language, the same format each quarter, and KRIs with thresholds so they see a risk growing before it becomes an incident.

interview.q: What are the limits of a 5×5 heat map?
interview.a: The scores are ordinal: a 20 is not exactly twice a 10, and 4 × 5 and 5 × 4 give the same score for very different risks. So I never average or add scores, I define every level of the scales in business terms, I record the reasons for each score, and I discuss the borderline cases. For the few decisions that need a money figure, I use ranges in money, for example with FAIR, rather than more precise-looking scores.
